label: text
text: BAD NOTES AT TAIPO MARKET.

label: text
text: UTTERER SENTENCED

label: text
text: The institution of Taipo market dealers led to the discomfiture of a would-be utterer of forged Hongkong and Shanghai Bank notes and finally to his appearance at the Criminal Sessions. On February 8, Lai Sau went to a salt fish dealer at Taipo Market and after purchasing a catty and a half of fish tendered a $10 note in payment. Asked if he had small change he replied in the negative and the dealer, examining the note, thought that it was different to those he had handled before and refused to accept. The man then left the stall without taking his purchase or paying for

label: text
text: At another, still further along, Lail Sau was again unsuccessful in his endeavour to get the stall holder to accept the note for some noodles. This was because the wife of the stall holder had noticed the trouble further up the street and he was not satisfied that the note was genuine.

label: text
text: After Lai Sau left his stall, the master informed a detective who followed Lai Sau to another salt fish store where again a $10 note was preferred for payment and refused. With the note in his hand, Lai Sau was arrested and when searched at Taipo police station five others were found on him, all six being forgeries.

label: text
text:
At the Criminal Sessions this morning Lai Sau was charged with uttering the forged note the detective saw him proffer and with possession of the other five, knowing them to have been forged. The prisoner's previous statement at Taipo was referred to by Mr. T. M. Hazlerigg, Crown Soldier, who prosecuted. In this statement, Lai Sau denied that he knew they were forged but begged the inspector to "excuse him this time." In future he would abide by the rules of Hongkong.
With regard to guilty knowledge which would have to be proved for the jury to return a verdict of guilty, Mr. Hazlerigg pointed to the fact of his persistence in attempts to get rid of the note and to the fact that he had refused to proffer small change whereas he had a genuine $1 note and $1.60 in genuine small money on him when arrested.
The notes found on prisoner were all made from the same plate as was evident from certain defects common to them all. From this and the facts mentioned, Mr. Hazlerigg asked the jury to find that prisoner knew the notes were forged and that he tendered the one intending to pass it off on the people of the New Territories, who were not greatly experienced in such matters.

label: text
text: Mr. William Beveridge was called for evidence as to the nature of the notes found on prisoner. They were all forgeries, he said. The defects common to them all pointed to their having been taken from the same plate.

label: text
text: Mr. Hazlerigg: Are they fairly colourable representations of the notes of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank?

label: text
text:
Mr. Beveridge: Yes, fairly.
Mr. Hazlerigg: If presented with a number of good notes are they calculated to mislead a person?

label: text
text: Mr. Beveridge: If counted at the corners, they might have been passed.

label: text
text: His Honour (Mr. Justice Wood): Would you say that the paper feels different and that the picture of the Bank on the back is not so clear as on genuine notes?

label: text
text: His Honour: Have you met others of this series?

label: text
text: Witness: Only one, a month of two ago.

label: text
text: His Lordship asked the Crown Solicitor if he had a genuine $10 note and on being smilingly assured that he had not, asked Mr. Beveridge if he had. Mr. Beveridge produced one and His Honour asked if he would mind leaving it as an exhibit in the case. It would be returned.

label: text
text: The juror found the prisoner guilty, and sentenced him to three years' imprisonment.

label: text
text:
A robbery at the Hong Kong Hospital, Cheung Chau led to the appearance of two Chinese at the Criminal Sessions this morning, both of whom pleaded not guilty. The robbery took place on February 7 when eight bangles, five pairs of silver earrings and a pair of jade stone earrings were stolen by three men who entered the servants quarters of the hospital at 11 p.m. and, terrorising the two women and a man who were there, took the articles and effected their escape. Shortly afterwards, two Indian constables who were on duty in the street, heard sounds of running and saw the two defendants come into sight. The constables stopped the men, one of whom was seen to throw away a bug which, when picked up was found to contain a bangle.

label: paragraph_title
text: RESTORED TO HUSBAND IN COURT:

label: text
text: AN ACTOR'S ELOPEMENT

label: text
text: How a Shantung actor eloped with a Javanese woman, the wife of a Hakka carpenter living at Shaukiwan Road, was described before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning. The woman was charged with the theft of a quantity of jewellery and $124 in money and the actor was charged with receiving the stolen property.

label: text
text: The second defendant said that the woman was passionately in love with him and although he was without money they managed to get along well for three months. His Worship (to send defendant): You have been living on love. What about the money; who provided you with food?

label: text
text: The husband of the woman, the complainant in the case, informed His Worship that he would for give his wife's lapse and take her back if she would be penitent. This being done, the couple were re-united, the woman being ordered to sign a bond to be of good behaviour.

label: text
text: The second defendant was sentenced to three months' hard labour.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: POLICE COURT CASE

label: text
text: Evidence at considerable length was taken before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning in a summons taken out by Mrs. V. L. Spink, of No. 211, Watchal Road, against Miss May Murray, living next door, for using abusive language. The complainant was represented by Mr. G. R. Haywood and Mr. A. J. O'Donoghue appeared for the defence.

label: text
text: Reference was made to the alleged use of obscene expressions by the defendant in the hearing of the complainant on two occasions which counsel described as the fortune telling and knitting needle incidents. One of the expressions alleged to have been used by the defendant which complainant wrote on paper and later admitted under cross-examination was that she was called "a bad egg."

label: text
text: At the conclusion of evidence given by Mrs. Blanche Jones (a witness for the complainant), and the father and sister of the defendant, His Worship bound both parties over to keep the peace for twelve months on bonds of $100 each.

PICKETS SURROUNDED & DISARMED.

label: text
text: 80 CASES OF BOMBS

label: text
text: Stirring events are believed to have occurred in Canton on Saturday, the most important of which was the surrounding of the Strike Headquarters and the disarming of a large number of boycott pickets.

label: text
text: No official confirmation of the reports had come to hand when the "China Mail" went to press. However, the best informed sources were of the opinion that there was substance for most of the conflicting drop of rumours. It has been definitely established that troops—said to be Cadets of General Chang Kai-shek's army landed at the East Bund on Saturday morning and proceeded to Tung Yuen (strikeheadquarters). A subsequent message says that the military have been withdrawn.

label: text
text: The strike (of boycott) pickets there were mostly disarmed, it is stated, when the troops arrived on the scene. The number of weapons taken is variously given, but it is believed that the majority of pickets had their arms taken from them.

label: text
text: Meanwhile troops were moving about in other parts of the city. The state of suspense lasted till the afternoon. During the period telephone communication was suspended. In parts of the city, military cordons held up traffic and then retired. Railway stations were also the scene of animation. For short while a rumour went around that Canton banknotes were being accepted but the scars said to have passed over quickly.

label: text
text: A vernacular report says that 100 soldiers were sent to Tung Zhen but a statement alleged to

label: text
text: Yuen but a statement, alleged to have emanated from the chairman of the strike committee, indicates that the troops were sent to a building adjoining Tung Yuen.

label: text
text: In the afternoon, Tung Yuen issued two notices emphasising that the movements referred to were only connected with military developments and that their normal course was thereby interrupted but the "position of labour" was not affected.

label: text
text: The coup—if it was one—also involved the Canton naval forces. Detachments were sent to the "Chung-Shan" (flagship) and other boats, and the vessels steamed up river. Naval headquarters, it is also rumoured were surrounded.

label: text
text: The guards posted at the Canton shell factory have been disarmed, according to several vernacular reports. One paper hints that the authorities allege that secret manual-factures have been detached, including 80 cases of bombs and some machine-guns.

label: text
text: Although official intelligence hits yet to arrive, the above re-forts are gaining strength in Hongkong.

label: text
text: One rumour which is not likely to mean much is that the family of a leading official has left Canton.

label: text
text: A Chinese was found in an unconscious condition at Queen Street yesterday. He was taken to the Government Civil Hospital and died after admittance.

label: text
text:
During blasting operations at the Government quarry at North Point on Saturday, a Chinese worker was killed by a flying fragment of rock striking him on the head.
The Chinese who was charged with the attempted theft of six tons of crude oil from the A.P.O. installation at North Point was sentenced to three months' hard labour at the Magistracy on Friday.
As the result of an accident in which a Chinese was injured near the Bowrington Canal on Saturday, a motor kerry driver and learner were formally charged at the Central Magistracy this morning and remained. It was stated that the injured man was in hospital and a charge of mania aughter might result if he were to life.

label: text
text: CONDITIONS LAST YEAR REVIEWED:

label: text
text: Interesting information is to be obtained in the chapter. "Local Progress in Wireless-Telegraphy in 1925" in the annual report of the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce, now being issued to members.

label: text
text: The “China Muil” has taken the following from an advance proof:—

label: text
text: The Chamber is indebted to the Public Works Department for the following notes on the development of Wireless Telegraphy during 1925:—

label: text
text:
"Interport traffic suffered considerably from the strike and boycott. The Canton service was discontinued on June 26, and has not since been resumed. Owing to the inability of the Swatow Station to maintain communication with Hongkong; the Swatow service was very irregular from January to the end of May. From June onwards a greatly improved service was maintained with the result that the volume of traffic increased considerably until it was found necessary to discontinue the service at the end of October. The Indo-China service has attracted a larger volume of traffic since the commencement of the direct service with Hanoi in October. The Yunnanfu service via Hanoi was opened on November 1, 1925. During December the Yunnanfu traffic increased 100 per cent.
"The volume of ordinary ship traffic remains about the same, the normal increase having been counterbalanced by the loss due to the unsettled conditions prevailing, which caused ships to be laid up or diverted to other trade"

text: "Further investigations have been made in connection with the Direction Finder, but no satisfactory results have been obtained and it is most probable that this service will have to be abandoned. Before doing so, however, every effort is being made to overcome the difficulties experienced."
